license: MIT (LICENSE, sha256-pinned to the SPDX text by test/repository.test.cjs:124-132)
whatItIs: A Claude Code / Codex / Cursor plugin holding 11 SKILL.md files (one core `technical-writing` plus 10 document-type skills), 2 subagent definitions (`agents/prose-reviewer.md`, `agents/doc-grounder.md`), 2 slash commands (`commands/prose-review.md`, `commands/ground-docs.md`), two eval JSON files, and one structural Node test. It is a house style guide written as agent instructions, not a measurement harness.
method: The core skill (plugins/technical-writer/skills/technical-writing/SKILL.md) states one principle: a document states current verified behavior, conclusion first, every claim traceable, every fact in exactly one home. It enforces that through four layers. (1) A pre-draft checkpoint the writer must fill in working notes: `Kind | Audience | Purpose | Non-goals` (SKILL.md:41-47). (2) A five-kind classification table - normative, descriptive, historical, runbook, reference - where the kind decides the *edit rule*, with the explicit claim that "update docs to match code" is wrong for two of the five (SKILL.md:71-83); normative docs found violated by code are never watered down, the violation becomes a finding. (3) Hard rules plus a rule-precedence ladder: truth and history outrank document-type exceptions, which outrank shared style, which an author's stated voice preference can override (SKILL.md:57-96). (4) Two reference files: references/truth.md is sourcing (file:line or pinned commit behind every load-bearing claim; `**[source wanted: ...]**` markers instead of invented citations; Measured / Sourced / Estimated confidence tiers at truth.md:18-25; "print the command behind a count and run it at HEAD" at truth.md:11), and references/style.md is prescription (average ~20 words, hard max 35 per sentence at style.md:7; a 27-row banned-constructions table at style.md:49-76 covering antithesis, rule of three, importance announcements, cursed vocabulary, trailing participles; no section under three paragraphs at style.md:84). Review is a separate skill (reviewing-technical-prose/SKILL.md) carrying a BLOCKER/WARNING/OBS severity mapping, a 16-item delivery checklist, and - the unusual part - a "Findings to leave alone" false-positive guard at lines 48-62 ("flag only when several signs coincide in the same paragraph"). The largest single file, documenting-legacy-codebases/SKILL.md (16 KB), is a campaign doctrine rather than a style guide: survey the system's surfaces first and derive the docs tree from the inventory, rank evidence (code at HEAD > tests > dated runtime evidence > commit history > names and comments as "testimony"), prove alive/dead/dormant by wiring search rather than assuming, split surprising-but-real behavior ("quirks", which go in the document) from suspected defects ("findings", one file:line line for the owner, no triage), keep a coverage ledger, and fan out one grounding agent per planned document pipelined into a fresh-eyes reviewer with explicit model tiers (mechanical small, extraction small-to-mid, judgment mid, never largest, escalate only on a bounce).
measures:
Mostly it prescribes. But it is not pure prescription - there are four real rulers, only one of which measures a document's effect on a reader, and that one measures skill descriptions, not documents.

PROVEN, with recorded results: plugins/technical-writer/evals/trigger-evals.json is a measurement that ran and recorded numbers. Its `method` field says: "Each query was routed by a haiku agent given the full 29-entry roster (19 skills ... plus 10 real distractor skills) and asked which single skill it would consult first. Proxy measurement of description quality, not of live-session triggering." 36 queries, each with `should: true|false` and an `accept` list of destinations; negatives are included (tw08 landing-page copy, tw09 a typo fix, tw10 REST-vs-GraphQL, tw11 summarize a Slack thread, tw12 proofread a LinkedIn post); one query is in Dutch (tw03). Results per skill with dates: technical-writing 12/12, reviewing-technical-prose 12/12, documenting-legacy-codebases 7/7 (re-measured 2026-08-22 against a 39-entry roster), diagramming-processes 4/4, documenting-contracts 4/4. Notes record "accepted as a correct alternate landing" where a query moved to a sibling.

PROVEN, no harness: plugins/technical-writer/evals/evals.json holds 8 behavior scenarios (adversarial prompts - "make it punchy and compelling", a Friday ticket dump, a postmortem under blame pressure) each with a prose `expected_output`. Every one has `"files": []` and `"assertions": []`, and nothing runs them: package.json has `"test": "node --test"`, and the only test file in the tree is test/repository.test.cjs, which is structural. So the behavior evals are unscored fixtures. They cannot fail and cannot regress.

Quantitative but about coverage, not comprehension: the coverage ledger (documenting-legacy-codebases/SKILL.md:82-91) records documented counts against inventory denominators per surface, each with the command behind it and a date; documenting-contracts/SKILL.md:103 makes endpoint and DTO counts denominators; truth.md:50 states the rule directly - "count documented items against total public items (endpoints, commands, config keys) rather than judging completeness by impression."

Mechanical doc-vs-repo fact checks in CI: test/repository.test.cjs:89-98 asserts every local Markdown link in every .md resolves on disk; :100-112 asserts the README's spelled-out skill count ("ten specialized skills") equals the actual directory count. That is a lie-detector derived from the repository, not a prose linter.

Nothing in the repository measures whether a reader understood a document. No reader profile, no question set, no right/wrong per question, no score on the documents the plugin produces.

transferable.approach: Distractor-roster routing eval: measure findability by asking a fresh cheap model (haiku) to route a realistic, badly-phrased user query among the real destinations plus ~10 deliberate distractors, scoring pass/total, with negative cases (should:false) and an `accept` list that tolerates a correct sibling landing.
transferable.whereItLives: plugins/technical-writer/evals/trigger-evals.json:1-20 (the `method` and `targets` blocks with dated pass/total) and the `queries` array, e.g. tw02 (two accepted destinations), tw03 (Dutch), tw08-tw12 (should:false negatives)
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse's audit already sends one fresh cheap model per question and scores right answers, and already has a `findability` failure class - but (judging only from the brief, I did not read terse's skill files) it scores comprehension on a fixed question set and has no negatives and no competing destinations. Negatives catch the opposite defect from the one terse measures: a section that grabs readers who should have gone elsewhere. The distractor set is what makes the number mean something rather than being a one-door test, and `accept` lists stop a correct-but-different landing from counting as a failure. It is the same shape as terse's ruler (fresh cheap seat, scored, dated, recorded in a file), so it composes rather than replaces.
transferable.collidesWith: Nothing. It extends the findability class of terse's audit; it does not touch the answer-key-from-code step or the revise passes.

transferable.approach: Bind a reviewer's or judge's verdict to the sha256 of the exact text it read: compute the digest first, stop and report on mismatch, and state the digest reviewed when none was given.
transferable.whereItLives: plugins/technical-writer/agents/prose-reviewer.md:15 ("When the dispatch names an expected SHA-256, compute it first (`shasum -a 256`); on mismatch, stop and report the mismatch instead of reviewing")
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse's revise ends in a 3-writer 2-judge bake-off. A judge that silently read a stale or wrong draft produces a verdict that looks like a measurement and is not one. Two lines of protocol make the binding checkable, and the digest is the thing you record next to the score.
transferable.collidesWith: Nothing; it is an integrity device on the bake-off, not a rule about wording.

transferable.approach: Coverage denominators derived from code: enumerate the public surfaces (endpoints, commands, config keys, entry points) with the command printed and run at HEAD, then measure documented/total per surface, dated, in a ledger beside the docs.
transferable.whereItLives: plugins/technical-writer/skills/documenting-legacy-codebases/SKILL.md:82-91 (the ledger), :20-29 (the inventory list and the count rule), skills/documenting-contracts/SKILL.md:103, skills/technical-writing/references/truth.md:11 and :50
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse already derives its answer key from the code, so the enumeration machinery is half there. A denominator turns "6 of 6 reader questions right" into a statement with a known scope: 6 of 6 over what fraction of the public surface. Without it, a document can score perfectly on six questions nobody chose adversarially.
transferable.collidesWith: The audit's scoring step, mildly but really. terse measures readers on purpose; a coverage percentage creates exhaustiveness pressure (documenting-contracts demands every endpoint, every field, every key), which is the direct enemy of a terse document. If taken, take it as a reported scope note on the audit, never as a target to raise.

transferable.approach: Mechanical repo-vs-doc fact checks in CI: assert every relative Markdown link resolves on disk, and assert any count stated in prose equals the count on disk.
transferable.whereItLives: test/repository.test.cjs:89-98 (link resolution over every .md) and :100-112 (README's spelled-out skill count vs directory count)
transferable.whyItMightWork: Both catch instances of terse's `lie` class that no reader question would surface, and both are decidable without judgment - they check the document against the repository, not the prose against a taste.
transferable.collidesWith: The already-rejected "CI punctuation gates" and prose linters, at first glance - but only at first glance. This asserts no style rule; it fact-checks two claim types against the filesystem. Record it as the narrow exception, not as a reopening of the linter question. The repository itself states the boundary, at references/truth.md:63: "Automate only the mechanically decidable rules ... State where the linter stops and judgment starts."

weaknesses:
The bulk of it is exactly the class terse already measured as losing. references/style.md is a 27-row banned-constructions table, a hard 35-word sentence cap (style.md:7), and a minimum-three-paragraph section rule (style.md:84) - hard per-sentence word limits and a machine-tell catalog, both already rejected here, and the README at lines 35-36 names its own sources as "Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing" and Diataxis. Internally the two prescriptions pull against each other: a per-sentence maximum plus a per-section minimum is pressure to pad.

The part that would be a real measurement is not wired. All 8 entries in evals/evals.json carry `"assertions": []`, there is no runner, and no results are recorded anywhere I read. The `expected_output` strings are judgments in prose ("every planted tell caught"), so even with a runner they would need a judge seat, which the repo does not define for this purpose.

The one measurement that did run is self-graded and never fails. Every target in trigger-evals.json is pass==total (12/12, 12/12, 7/7, 4/4, 4/4), and the `note` fields retroactively widen what counts as correct: rp06 routing to writing-postmortems is "accepted as a correct alternate landing", tw02 moving to documenting-legacy-codebases likewise, and an acknowledged over-trigger is "tolerated". A ruler adjusted after reading the result is a weak ruler. I did not re-run it, so I cannot say the numbers are wrong - only that they are unfalsifiable as published.

The `model: sonnet` pin in both agent frontmatters (agents/prose-reviewer.md:4, agents/doc-grounder.md:4) is a fixed cost per document with no measured justification in the repo.

And the whole thing is young and small: 16 stars, created 2026-08-19, last pushed 2026-08-30, one author, no external contributors visible in the metadata I pulled.
